summary:
AstroPixel: Mission Designer is a free browser game where players design a space mission, fly it, and find out exactly why it worked or failed. Players pick one of eight destinations, from the Moon to Neptune, and build a spacecraft from 29 parts, which means every choice affects mass, power, fuel, data, budget and time. After that, they fly the launch, survive the cruise and land or orbit at their target. When a mission fails, the report shows which decision caused it, so players can fix it and fly again.
The game is built on NASA data. Gravity, sunlight and distance come from the NASA planetary fact sheets, the design margins follow JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels, the engine numbers come from NASA GMAT, and real 2024 solar storms from NASA’s DONKI database hit the ship during cruise. Values we chose for gameplay are labelled as game rules. We also built a team mode for up to four players, each taking a mission role. Overall, AstroPixel lets students learn how a whole mission works by doing it, not just reading about it
details:
What it does and how it works
AstroPixel: Mission Designer is a free browser game where players design a complete space mission, fly it, and find out exactly why it worked or failed. First, the player picks one of eight destinations, from Mercury to Neptune, and a task with an Easy, Normal or Hard difficulty. Then they choose a rocket and a flight path and build a spacecraft from 29 parts, such as solar arrays, nuclear power, batteries, antennas, instruments, landing gear, rovers and fuel. Every part has a mass, power use, cost and data value, so adding one instrument also means more power, more fuel and a bigger rocket. Mission Control shows a lamp for each system, and it only turns green when NASA’s design margin is kept. After that, the player flies the launch, survives the cruise, lands or reaches orbit, and explores with a rover or a drone. At the end, a report gives four scores and shows which decision caused each problem, so the player can fix the design and fly again.

NASA data
Gravity, sunlight and distance for each world come from the NASA planetary fact sheets. The design margins (35% on power, a 3 dB radio link) follow JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels paper. The engine efficiency comes from NASA GMAT’s default thruster. The nuclear power part uses the NASA MMRTG fact sheet. During the cruise, real 2024 solar storms from NASA’s DONKI database hit the ship. These values run through real physics: the rocket equation, and sunlight and radio signal falling with distance squared. Every number in the game shows its source, and values we chose for gameplay are labelled as game rules.

Benefits and intended impact
Students usually learn orbits, rockets and power in separate courses, and they rarely see how these parts affect each other in one mission. AstroPixel lets them experiment with a whole mission and fail safely, which is something real teams can only learn by losing real spacecraft. It runs in any browser with no install and no account, so a teacher can share one link with a whole class. This is important for us in Palestine, where we could not find an aerospace engineering degree and hands-on space learning is rare.

Tools and technologies

  • Game: Godot 4.7.2 and GDScript, exported to WebAssembly and hosted on GitHub Pages. There is also a Windows build.
  • Online team mode: a small Node.js relay server.
  • Art and sound: generated by our own scripts, with no AI image generators.
  • Website: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • Source data and tools: NASA planetary fact sheets, DONKI, GMAT and the JPL Concept Maturity Levels paper.

Creativity
Unlike Kerbal Space Program, every choice costs budget, power, data and time, and every number has a source. Unlike NASA’s Webb game, players run the whole mission on eight worlds, alone or in an online team mode for up to four players, each taking a role (Planner, Engineer, Scientist or Comms). NASA’s real margins decide GO or NO-GO, messages from Earth arrive late like real ones, and decision events are based on real missions such as Mars Climate Orbiter.

Factors we considered
We tried to keep the science honest while keeping the game playable. Because of that, the game is 2D and uses simplified physics instead of full orbits, and every invented value is labelled as a game rule. We also considered access: it works on school computers and phones with no login. We asked mentors and colleagues to test the game during and after development. Most of the feedback was positive, and we changed the game based on their suggestions, for example by rebuilding the spacecraft builder because testers found it too complicated.SS
